title: Formal Languages, Encodings, and Decision Problems

items.title: Computation alphabets, words, the empty word, and $\Sigma^*$
The computation-word convention agrees with the published finite-word definition
items.strategy: Let $\Sigma$ be finite. Unpack the local definition of a word of length $n$ as a function $n\to\Sigma$ and compare it term-for-term with [[def-finite-words-factor-avoidance-and-prefix-states]]. The only real work is to note that both pages use the same empty word and the same offset concatenation, so the underlying set $\Sigma^*$ is literally the same set and not merely a canonically isomorphic copy.

items.title: Languages over an alphabet
Boolean operations on languages over a fixed alphabet
Language concatenation, powers, and Kleene star
Language concatenation is associative
items.strategy: For $w\in (L_1L_2)L_3$, choose witnesses $u\in L_1$, $v\in L_2$, and $x\in L_3$ with $w=(uv)x$. The offset definition of word concatenation makes $((uv)x)(i)$ and $(u(vx))(i)$ equal for every position $i$, so $(uv)x=u(vx)$. This gives $w\in L_1(L_2L_3)$, and the reverse inclusion is symmetric.

items.title: Kleene star is the least concatenation-closed language containing $L$ and $\varepsilon$
items.strategy: Show directly that $\varepsilon\in L^*$ and $LL^*\subseteq L^*$. Then prove by induction that any language $K$ with $\varepsilon\in K$ and $LK\subseteq K$ contains every $L^n$. A separate factor-count argument gives $L^*L^*\subseteq L^*$, so $L^*$ is itself the least concatenation-closed language containing $L$ and $\varepsilon$.

items.title: Word reversal and language reversal
Reversal is an involution and reverses concatenation
items.strategy: Prove the word identities first. Induct on the length of the second factor to show $(uv)^R=v^Ru^R$, using the defining clause $(wa)^R=aw^R$. A second induction on length gives $(w^R)^R=w$. The language statements then follow pointwise from the definition $L^R=\{w^R:w\in L\}$.

items.title: Alphabet maps into $\Delta^*$ and their induced maps on words
The induced word map is the unique concatenation-preserving extension
items.strategy: Let $h:\Sigma\to\Delta^*$ be the alphabet map of the definition and let $\widehat h:\Sigma^*\to\Delta^*$ be its induced map. Prove $\widehat h(uv)=\widehat h(u)\widehat h(v)$ by induction on the length of $v$ and the explicit block-concatenation definition of $\widehat h$. For uniqueness, let $g:\Sigma^*\to\Delta^*$ preserve concatenation and agree with $h$ on one-letter words. Induct on word length: the empty word must map to $\varepsilon$, and a nonempty word splits as $ua$, so $g(ua)=g(u)g(a)=\widehat h(u)h(a)=\widehat h(ua)$.

items.title: Effective binary encodings and total decoders
Finite tuples admit effective prefix-free binary encodings
items.strategy: Use an explicit self-delimiting code for a single binary word, for example $c(w)=1^{|w|}0w$. Then encode a tuple $(w_1,\dots,w_k)$ as $1^k0\,c(w_1)\cdots c(w_k)$. Decode by first reading the initial unary block to recover $k$, then parse exactly $k$ self-delimiting word blocks. Prefix-freeness comes from the first block determining the tuple length and each subsequent block determining its own endpoint.

items.title: Decision problems, search problems, and function problems
Instance size and polynomially related encodings
Polynomially related encodings preserve polynomial size bounds
items.strategy: Given a polynomial bound in one encoding, first replace that bound polynomial by a nondecreasing polynomial majorant. Then compose with the comparison polynomial from polynomial relatedness to transfer the bound to the other encoding, and argue symmetrically in the reverse direction.

items.title: FALSE: a language is a set of symbols
items.strategy: Refute the claim on the binary alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ with the language $L=\{01\}$. The element $01$ is a word of length two, so $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ is a language, but $01\notin\Sigma$. The falsehood is exactly the design's syntax-versus-denotation warning: a language is a set of words over an alphabet, not a subset of the alphabet itself.

items.title: FALSE: every effective encoding is prefix-free
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the binary encoding $e(w)=1w$. It is injective, and the total decoder that strips the first bit on inputs beginning with $1$ and returns a fixed malformed-code token otherwise decodes it effectively. But the image is not prefix-free: $e(\varepsilon)=1$ is a prefix of $e(0)=10$.

title: Formal Languages, Encodings, and Decision Problems: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A concrete calculation of $(L_1L_2)L_3=L_1(L_2L_3)$
items.strategy: Take $L_1=\{a\}$, $L_2=\{\varepsilon,b\}$, and $L_3=\{a,bb\}$ over $\{a,b\}$. Compute $L_1L_2=\{a,ab\}$ and then $(L_1L_2)L_3=\{aa,abb,aba,abbb\}$. Compute $L_2L_3=\{a,bb,ba,bbb\}$ and then $L_1(L_2L_3)=\{aa,abb,aba,abbb\}$. The example should exhibit the same four words on both sides rather than only appealing to the general lemma.

items.title: Ordinary binary numerals and doubled-bit numerals are polynomially related
items.strategy: Encode a natural number $n$ first by its standard binary numeral $\sigma(n)$ and second by the doubled-bit code $\tau(n)$ obtained by replacing each bit by two copies. Then $|\tau(n)|=2|\sigma(n)|$ for every $n$, so the two encodings are polynomially related in the strongest possible way. Check a concrete instance such as $13$, where $\sigma(13)=1101$ and $\tau(13)=11110011$, and then show how a bound like $|\tau(n)|^3$ translates back to $8|\sigma(n)|^3$.

items.title: The language $\{01\}$ is not a set of alphabet symbols
items.strategy: Use the binary alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. The one-element set $L=\{01\}$ is a language because $01\in\Sigma^*$, but it is not a subset of $\Sigma$ because $01$ is a word of length two rather than a single symbol. Write both containments explicitly: $01\in\Sigma^*$ and $01\notin\Sigma$.

items.title: The encoding $w\mapsto 1w$ is effective but not prefix-free
items.strategy: Take the encoding $e(w)=1w$ on binary strings. The decoder reads the first bit: if it is $1$, remove it and output the remainder; if it is $0$ or the string is empty, return the fixed malformed-code output. This shows effectiveness directly. Prefix-freeness fails because $1=e(\varepsilon)$ is a proper prefix of $10=e(0)$.
